newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FORECAST-Lion H1 earnings seen drained.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Lion H1 earnings seen drained.

text.p: Unrelenting competition in a declining Australasian beer market is expected to weigh heavily on New Zealand-based Lion Nathan Ltd when it reports its first half result next week, analysts said on Monday.
Bad weather that depressed consumption over the seasonally important summer period would also be a factor, they said.
Analysts expect the Australasian beer and beverage giant to report a net profit of between NZ$67-69 million for the six months to February, down from NZ$91.2 million a year earlier.
Lion said in March it expected to report a two to three percent drop in beer sales over the half and predicted a drop of four to five percent over the year.

The company cited very poor weather, especially in Auckland, declining per capita consumption, increased discretionary spending on gaming, the anti drink-drive campaign on television and increased random breath testing as reasons for the fall.

But Lion chief executive Douglas Myers told Reuters in an interview earlier this month that Lion's Australian market share of about 42 percent had stabilised. Analysts expect to find out from next week's result exactly how this was achieved.
John Cairns at Cavill White Securities said discounting may have been a factor in the turnaround.

"From what we hear it is from discounting their brands, but they would say that pricing is an integral part of managing the particular brand," he said. In Australia, Lion's arch rival is Foster Brewing Group's Carlton United Breweries.
Analysts said there appeared to be no light at the end of the tunnel for Lion's underperforming Pepsi joint venture in Australia, in which it has an 83.54 percent interest.
The venture, which the company has said it could consider selling, is expected to turn in a loss before interest and tax.
Analysts believe it is still too early in the development of Lion's brewing interests in China for them to make any meaningful contribution and that there were risks there too.
"It's not an easy ride in China and they are certainly not the only party to have entered the fray, so I guess the jury is still out on that," Cairns said.
Lion is also facing stiff competition at home from a rejuvenated DB Group Ltd, and New Zealand is expected to return a lower contribution.
"All in all it is not an overly positive position," Cairns said, although he noted the share price had held up well.
Lion traded today at NZ$3.45, down three cents,
Warren Doak at Merrill Lynch said there had been a sharp decline in beer volumes for the quarter ending in February and he expected an annualised decline in volume of about six percent.
He also took issue with on an often-expressed view that Lion Nathan is cheap when valued against its international peers.
"The fundamentals of the markets in which Lion operates possibly indicate that Lion deserves to be on that sort of discount, given its growth profile," Doak said.

"But it is a turnaround story. If Lion can recapture market share in the low alcohol sector -- in other words bringing out the next innovative product -- then there is every opportunity for them," he said.
